# blitz-recompiler: feasibility and design

Status: findings from analysing two executables of the same program (Stranded II, source in `tests/stranded2`): one built by the original Blitz3D 1.107 (PE timestamp 2010-10-12) and one built by the Blitz3D_Soloud fork (2024-08-30). The proof of concept is `tools/blitz_exe_info.py`.

## Recommendation: go

The program part of a Blitz executable is easy to find, is a clean relocatable module with its symbol names intact, and is produced by a small template code generator. A purpose-built lifter is realistic; a general-purpose x86 lifter is not needed. The hard parts are the 32-bit/64-bit mismatch for strings and objects, x87 floating point, and user library (DLL) calls, none of which block a first version.

Only recompile executables you have the right to modify and redistribute: freeware, your own programs, or programs whose owner allows it. The tool must not circumvent protection of commercial releases, and the README should say so.

## 1. What an executable looks like

Both builds have the same shape. They are 32-bit PE files with a statically linked runtime (about 0.9 MB of `.text`, imports of DirectDraw, DirectInput, DirectSound-era WinMM, WinSock, and so on) and one resource: **RT_RCDATA id 1111**, about 3 MB, which is the compiled program. Everything else is the original runtime, which BlitzLLVM replaces.

| Part | Where | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Startup stub | PE entry point | Calls the runtime's `_bbWinMain`, which loads resource 1111, resolves its symbols and jumps to `__MAIN`. |
| Command table | `.text` | Built at start-up by `push <fn>; push <"Name%arg$arg2=default">; call rtSym` sequences. A scan finds about 580 to 600 entries; the rest use other call forms. Not needed, since BlitzLLVM already has `builtins.inc`. |
| Program | resource 1111 | See below. |
| Debug info | none in release builds | Debug builds call `_bbDebugEnter/Leave/Stmt` and carry statement tables. Not seen in the samples. |

### The program module (resource 1111)

```
u32  code_size
u8   code[code_size]        x86 machine code and data, base 0, position independent apart from relocations
u32  n; { cstr name; u32 offset } * n     labels (definitions)
u32  n; { cstr name; u32 offset } * n     relocations against names, 4 byte slot at offset (calls: rel32, data: abs32)
u32  n; { cstr name; u32 offset } * n     relocations against names, 4 byte slot at offset (absolute data addresses)
```

The file ends exactly at the third table, so detection is exact: the sizes must add up. The format is identical in the 2010 and 2024 builds.

The names are what makes this tractable. For Stranded II:

| Prefix | Meaning | Count |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `_f<name>` | Blitz function (also the name of a runtime command when it is not defined here) | 658 defined |
| `_v<name>` | global variable | 690 |
| `_a<name>` | global `Dim` array | 247 |
| `_t<name>` | `Type` descriptor | 61 |
| `_<number>` | local jump labels, `_<n>_begin` and `_<n>_leave` bracket functions | 20 698 |
| `__MAIN`, `__LIBS`, `__DATA` | start of main program, user library declarations, `Data` table | 3 |

External references of the whole 1.5 MB program are only **336 names**:

* 36 compiler support functions: `__bbStr{Load,Store,Const,Concat,Compare,Release,ToInt,ToFloat,FromInt,FromFloat,ToCStr}`, `__bbCStrToStr`, `__bbObj{New,Delete,Store,Release,First,Last,Next,Prev,InsBefore,InsAfter,EachFirst,EachNext,Compare,ToHandle,FromHandle}`, `__bbDimArray`, `__bbUndimArray`, `__bbRestore`, `__bbLoadLibs`, `__bbFPow`, `__bbFMod`, `__bbFAbs`, `__bbAbs`, `__bbMod`.
* 300 runtime commands, as `_f<lowercase command name>`. 299 are in BlitzLLVM's `builtins.inc` (the missing one is `End`, which is a keyword here).
* 3 type tags (`__bbIntType`, `__bbFltType`, `__bbStrType`).

The two builds reference the same 336 names. The command signature (`EntityX%entity%global=0`) is in the original stub, but BlitzLLVM already knows it.

### Code generation style

The original compiler is a simple template generator, which is why lifting is feasible:

* 78 distinct mnemonics over 378 000 instructions, and only about 45 are real (the rest are misdecoded constant data between functions). All 658 function bodies disassemble cleanly. There is no self-modifying or packed code in the samples.
* Every function: `push ebx/esi/edi/ebp; mov ebp,esp; sub esp,N`, locals at `[ebp-4*k]`, parameters at `[ebp+0x14+4*k]`, callee pops its arguments (`ret N`), result in `eax`.
* Calls to commands and support functions: `sub esp,N; mov [esp+4*k],value; call rel32` (relocation at `call+1`).
* Floats are 32-bit and travel through integer registers and stack slots as bit patterns; arithmetic uses the x87 stack (`fld/fild/fstp/fistp`, `faddp/fsubp/fsubrp/fmulp/fdivp`, `fchs`, `fucompp; fnstsw ax; sahf; seta`). The values are rounded back to 32 bit with `fstp dword` after each statement.
* Strings are runtime-owned pointers; the program only passes them to `__bbStr*`. Objects (`Type` instances) are pointers to a block whose fields the program reads at constant offsets (`mov eax,[eax]; add eax,8`), with strings and objects in 4 byte slots. Everything else (images, entities, banks, files) is an `Int` handle.
* Only three indirect calls (`call eax`) in the whole program, which are the user library calls (`__LIBS` lists `user32.dll` clipboard functions for Stranded II).

## 2. Approaches

### A. Lift the module to LLVM IR with a small purpose-built lifter (recommended)

Read the module with the parser in `tools/blitz_exe_info.py`, split into functions at the `_f` labels, and translate the template instruction subset to LLVM IR (registers as SSA values or allocas; `[ebp-x]` as allocas; `esp` frame as a per-call alloca; x87 as a modelled 8 slot stack, which the templates keep very shallow). Each `call rel32` against a name becomes a call to a thunk. Then link the result with the BlitzLLVM runtime exactly like compiler output. This reuses the existing optimizer, linker, cross compiling and the runtime.

Boundary mapping:

* **Commands** `_f<name>` map to the `bb_*` symbol in `builtins.inc`, with the stack arguments loaded in order; float arguments are bitcast from the 32-bit slots. Needs the name to be the same table the compiler uses (a generated header would avoid drift).
* **Strings** are the real mismatch: the runtime uses `const char*` (64 bit). Options: (1) implement `__bbStr*` and `__bbObj*` inside the recompiler's own support library, with strings as 32-bit handles into a table, and convert at the command thunk (copy in, copy out); (2) place all program-visible memory in the low 4 GB. Option 1 is cleaner and portable. The support functions are tiny (36) and the semantics are documented by the original source (blitz3d is open source).
* **Objects** are only accessed through offsets from the `__bbObj*` results, so the support library can keep the same 32-bit layout (`next/prev/fields...`) in an arena addressed by 32-bit offsets; `Handle`/`Object` use `__bbObjToHandle` and `__bbObjFromHandle`.
* **Data**: absolute relocations (`_v...`, `_a...`, `_t...`, `__DATA`) are offsets into the module image, which stays in a flat 32-bit address arena. Loads and stores become `base + zext(address)`.
* **Floating point**: model st(i) as `double` with rounding to `float` at `fstp dword`. The originals run with x87 extended precision, so tiny differences are possible; `x86_fp80` can be used as an exact mode on x86 hosts.
* **User libraries**: `__LIBS` lists DLL functions (`name.dll\0Func\0...`). On Windows these can be called through a generated trampoline; elsewhere only a built-in replacement table works, otherwise the recompiler must report which libraries are missing and refuse.

Estimated effort: parser and loader (done in the proof of concept), x86 subset decoder plus IR emitter (about 45 mnemonics), support library, runtime thunk generator, driver. Probably 3 to 4 weeks for a first working Stranded II.

### B. Decompile to Blitz source and use the normal compiler

The names and the template code make function bodies recoverable, but local variable names, field names, type declarations and expression structure are lost (the compiler flattens `If`/`For`/`Select` into labels), and variable types must be inferred. Readable output needs a structuring pass. It would give the best result for maintenance but is far more work for uncertain fidelity. Not recommended as the first step, though the symbol recovery is a reasonable stretch goal.

### C. General lifter (remill, McSema, Rev.ng)

Heavy dependencies, designed for arbitrary binaries and gives unreadable IR with the full flag model and the Windows PE runtime. The instruction subset here is small and uniform, so a purpose-built lifter is smaller than the integration cost. Not recommended.

### D. Emulate or run the original runtime

Out of scope: it would not use the BlitzLLVM runtime, which is the goal.

## 3. Risks

* **Unknown dialects**: BlitzPlus and Blitz2D/BlitzBasic modules, older Blitz3D builds and other forks (Soloud, ...) must be checked; module layout and symbol prefixes may differ. The proof of concept detects them rather than assuming.
* **Compiler optimization**: none of the original compilers optimize, but other tooling (packers such as UPX or exe protectors) can hide resource 1111; the tool should report them and stop.
* **User libraries and `Decls`**: need an FFI story, see above.
* **Runtime semantic differences** (the Differences page): behavior that a program relies on and BlitzLLVM deliberately changed. Same as for source builds.
* **Strings with embedded NUL or binary data**: the original string is length-counted, the BlitzLLVM runtime uses C strings; commands such as `ReadString` are affected equally for source builds.
* **Debug builds**: the statement table and `_bbDebug*` calls need mapping or removal.
* **Legal**: see the recommendation. Recompiling does not change who holds the rights, so only run it on programs you may modify.

## 4. Proof of concept

`python3 tools/blitz_exe_info.py program.exe [--functions] [--commands] [--disasm NAME]` detects a Blitz executable (exact module size check), lists the program's functions, globals, arrays and types, the support functions it needs, and checks every runtime command against `builtins.inc`. For both Stranded II builds: 658 functions, 690 globals, 247 arrays, 61 types, 36 support functions, 300 commands of which 299 are in `builtins.inc` (the last is `End`). `--disasm` needs the optional `capstone` module and annotates each reference with its symbol name. Output for both builds is in the pull request description.

Not done: lifting. Per the task, that is the next decision.

## 5. Task breakdown

1. Module reader as a C++ library in `code_tools` (port of the Python parser; sizes and symbols). Plus a detector for BlitzPlus and older Blitz3D executables; check more samples.
2. Generate the command mapping table (name, symbol, signature) from `builtins.inc` for the recompiler, so the two cannot drift.
3. x86 decoder for the template subset, with a "reject anything else" mode, so unknown code is reported instead of mistranslated.
4. IR emitter for integer code, calls and control flow; test with a handful of tiny programs compiled by the original compiler (`Print "Hello"`, loops, recursion).
5. x87 modelling and float tests (compare against the original on a set of math programs).
6. Support library: strings, objects and types, `Dim`, `Data`/`Restore`, `Handle`, with the 32-bit arena.
7. Thunk generator for commands, strings in/out, userlib/FFI handling.
8. `blitz-recompiler` driver: input exe, output exe/IR (`-S`), diagnostics for unsupported modules.
9. Stranded II as the first full test: both builds must run, compared to the source build in `tests/stranded2`.
10. Wiki page and README note, including the legal paragraph.
